claims.text: The proposed method combines active-learning machine-learning potentials with enhanced sampling such as replica exchange or metadynamics.
The hybrid method will provide near-ab-initio accuracy for complete fusion free energies.
The computed fusion free energies will faithfully include vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron-vibration coupling.
The hybrid method will substantially reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio workflows.
The intended systems include elemental materials, binary alloys, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys in both solid and liquid phases.
A minimal set of high-fidelity ab initio calculations is sufficient to train the active-learning potential.
Enhanced sampling will efficiently explore the free-energy landscapes of both solid and liquid phases.
The proposed test domain is approximately 0.9–1.1 times the melting temperature.
The method is proposed to apply across compositions ranging from elemental and binary systems to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The machine-learning potential can capture the electronic, vibrational, and anharmonic features needed for the relevant free-energy landscape.
Enhanced sampling ensures accurate phase-space exploration.
Replacing full-scale ab initio molecular dynamics with a trained potential reduces the number of expensive calculations.
The trained-potential workflow will still resolve detailed solid-liquid free-energy differences.
The method may achieve orders-of-magnitude speedup over explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
Fusion free energies, melting temperatures, and latent heats will remain within acceptable ab initio error margins.
The hybrid method will be faster than TOR-TILD, particularly for complex multicomponent systems.
Uncertainty increases when the method is applied far outside the near-melting temperature and stated composition domain.
Extreme anharmonicity and electron-vibration coupling in complex systems may require further calibration of the machine-learning potential.
